content: The inclusion of food items from various countries within each major geographic region was feasible. However, mixed dishes were excluded from the food item list due to their wide variability globally. Instead, whenever possible, the ingredients of mixed dishes were included if researchers had previously disaggregated these dishes into their component parts in the data sources. The available datasets and food item lists varied in this regard. The development of the food item list involved several steps: 1. Extracting food item lists from diverse sources. 2. Excluding rarely consumed items, defined as those consumed by fewer than 5% of infants and young children in most cases. 3. Categorically excluding certain items, such as condiments and mixed dishes (details in Annex 3). 4. Categorizing food items into food groups and subgroups. 5. Matching each food item to an appropriate entry in a food composition database. During this process, less healthy items were matched to healthier alternatives (e.g., fried meats were matched to stewed or braised meats, and processed cheese foods were matched to unprocessed cheese). Fortified items were matched to non-fortified equivalents due to the global variability in fortification levels. The initial focus was on identifying gaps in unfortified diets, with fortified items for infants and young children added later in the modeling process. The final food item list included 404 items, representing foods consumed by infants and young children in 37 countries. However, 24 of these items lacked sufficient specificity to match them to nutrient values (e.g., if the data source only indicated fish). As a result, the food composition database included 380 unique items with nutrient values. For sentinel unhealthy items, three commonly consumed types were identified: sugar-sweetened beverages, sweet biscuits, and fried crisps or chips. Nutrient profiles for these items were averaged across several examples. For instance, sugar-sweetened beverages were represented by an average of nutrient data from a juice drink and a sugar-sweetened carbonated drink (soda). Fortified items included in the analysis, based on input from the Guideline Development Group (GDG), were: Multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs). Small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS). Fortified cereal-based products targeted at infants and young children (e.g., Super Cereal Plus). Food composition data were sourced primarily from U.S. databases, supplemented with data from other countries (e.g., Germany) for unfortified items when necessary. In cases where no suitable match was found in U.S. databases, other national or regional databases were consulted, such as the ASEAN food composition database for certain Asian fruits. Nutrient profiles for food subgroups were calculated by averaging nutrient values across all countries where the food item was consumed. Items consumed in more countries were given greater weight in the calculations. For example, carrots, consumed in 27 of 37 countries, had nearly double the weight of pumpkin, consumed in 15 countries, when calculating the average nutrient profile for vitamin A-rich orange vegetables. The modeling process aimed to minimize nutrient gaps while ensuring feasibility. Maximum quantities and frequencies of consumption were defined for food groups and subgroups based on observed data. For example, the maximum daily serving size for each food subgroup was based on median daily intakes in settings with the highest consumption. Weekly consumption patterns were modeled rather than daily ones, allowing flexibility in selecting subgroups within a food group while adhering to feasible totals. For fluid milk, maximum quantities were set cautiously to avoid displacing breast milk, particularly for infants under 12 months. The feasible best-case food patterns reflected settings where food subgroups were consumed more frequently or in larger quantities. In cases where nutrient gaps remained, liberalized best-case patterns were explored, allowing for higher weekly consumption frequencies. Sentinel unhealthy items and fortified items were modeled separately. For unhealthy items, daily serving sizes were based on the highest observed median intakes. For fortified items, fixed amounts were used (e.g., one sachet of MNP or SQ-LNS). These items were not considered part of the core food groups, except for Super Cereal Plus, which was coded as a staple food. The Optifood software was used to minimize nutrient gaps between modeled solutions and nutrient reference values (NRVs) for target nutrients. In scenarios where all target NRVs were met, the software minimized protein as a secondary objective, serving as a proxy for reducing diet costs in resource-constrained environments.
